implementation_notes: The JDK ships the identity function as a typed factory: Function.identity() (static, since Java 8) returns a Function<T,T> that always returns its input argument, and its UnaryOperator<T> specialization exposes the same factory for the a-to-a shape demanded by Stream.map, iterate steps and similar operator slots; Collectors.toMap and groupingBy take it directly as key or value extractor - the Collectors API note explicitly recommends Function.identity() when the element itself is the key. Because lambda bodies are inlined by the JIT, the neutral element costs nothing at the call site, and composition laws hold through Function.compose/andThen: f.compose(id) and id.andThen(f) behave as f. The classic hand-written form stays justified for custom SAM types or non-Function targets, where a local lambda t -> t with the right target type (or a private static <T> UnaryOperator<T> id() helper) is the idiom; the binary comparator identity has no stdlib form - Comparator.comparing(Function.identity()) orders by the element itself and requires Comparable elements.
pitfalls: Function.identity() is typed Function<T,T>; where the target is UnaryOperator, BinaryOperator or a custom SAM, inference fails or the assignment is a compile error - use the matching factory (UnaryOperator.identity()) or an explicit type witness.

Comparator.comparing(Function.identity()) is not a (a, b) -> 0 no-op comparator: it extracts the element itself as the sort key, so sorting a non-Comparable type passes compilation (with an inference witness) and only fails as ClassCastException at sort time.

Collectors.toMap(Function.identity(), v -> v) throws IllegalStateException on duplicate keys: identity as key extractor makes equal elements collide - supply the three-argument toMap with a merge function when duplicates are legal.

identity() returns the same reference, so an identity map step on mutable objects shares state with the source - pass-through is not a defensive copy, and downstream mutation is visible to the original.
